name: Shobha
definition: Shobha is a composite portrait of a woman working in Channapatna's traditional toy-craft economy, navigating import competition, household pressures and the costs of educating children. She reflects the lived experience of artisan families in Ramanagara district, where lacquerware heritage meets economic uncertainty and the pull of nearby Bengaluru's opportunities.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Shobha works in a small toy-painting unit near Channapatna town, where she applies colour to wooden animals, tops and rattles turned on lathes by men in the workshop. She earns roughly ₹7,000 a month, paid by the piece; in a good month when orders arrive from Bengaluru gift shops or government handicraft emporiums, she takes home a little more. The workshop owner complains constantly about Chinese plastic toys flooding the market and undercutting prices, and several units have closed in recent years. Shobha starts at eight and finishes by five, with an hour's break for lunch she carries from home. The smell of lacquer and sawdust clings to her saree; her fingers are stained yellow and red from dyes that do not wash off easily. Her husband drives an autorickshaw on the Channapatna-Ramanagara route and farms a small plot of coconut and ragi inherited from his father. Together they manage, but every month is tight: fuel for the auto, school fees, clinic visits, groceries from the weekly market, loan repayments for the auto and the borewell they sank two years ago when the rains failed.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Shobha lives in a two-room house on the edge of Channapatna town with her husband, her mother-in-law, and their two children—a daughter in eighth standard and a son in fifth. Her mother-in-law, now in her sixties, used to do the same painting work but her eyesight has weakened and she stays home to cook and mind the house. Shobha's husband leaves early for the auto stand and returns late, often after dark; some nights he sleeps in the auto near the town bus stand to catch early morning passengers. Shobha's day begins at five-thirty: she lights the stove, makes rice and sambar, packs tiffin for the children and her husband, then walks twenty minutes to the workshop. Her daughter helps with washing dishes and looking after her younger brother in the evenings; Shobha worries that the girl is taking on too much responsibility too young. Her own mother, widowed, lives in a village near Maddur and Shobha visits her once a month, taking the KSRTC bus under the Shakti scheme. Marriage in her family happened early—Shobha was nineteen—but she hopes her daughter will finish PUC before any talk of marriage begins.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Shobha studied only until seventh standard; her parents pulled her out to help at home when her younger siblings were born, and she regrets the lost years. Her daughter attends the government high school in Channapatna town, a ten-minute walk from home; the fees are low but the family pays for private tuition in mathematics and science—₹1,500 a month—because the school's results have been slipping and Shobha is determined the girl will pass SSLC with a first class. Her son goes to the same school's primary section. Both children speak Kannada at home and study in Kannada medium; the daughter wants to continue to PUC and perhaps join a nursing course in Ramanagara or even Bengaluru, though Shobha is not sure how they will afford hostel fees. Some families in the neighbourhood send their children to private English-medium schools in Ramanagara town, but that costs ₹20,000–25,000 a year and Shobha's household cannot stretch that far. The Shakti free-bus scheme has made it easier for her daughter to travel to Ramanagara for tuition on Sundays, and Shobha sees that as a lifeline: the girl will go further than she did.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Shobha's mother-in-law has diabetes and high blood pressure; every month they buy her medicines—₹800–1,000—from the town pharmacy because the government hospital often runs out of stock. Shobha herself has chronic back pain from sitting bent over the painting table, and her eyes ache by evening under the workshop's dim tube lights. She has been to the government taluk hospital in Channapatna twice in the past year—once for an infected finger cut by a splinter, once for her son's fever—and the doctors were helpful but the wait was long, sometimes three hours. For anything serious, families go to Ramanagara or Bengaluru; her husband's uncle had a heart problem last year and was taken straight to a private hospital in Ramanagara, and the family is still repaying that loan. Shobha's children are healthier than she was at their age—both have been vaccinated, the anganwadi worker was regular when they were small, and the school mid-day meal is reliable—but her daughter is thin and often tired, and Shobha wonders if she is anaemic. She has not had time or money to take the girl for a blood test. Shobha herself has never had a full health check-up; she goes to the doctor only when something hurts too much to ignore.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Shobha's family is Vokkaliga, part of a large extended network in and around Channapatna; her husband's cousins and uncles all work in toy-making, farming or transport. The family's social life revolves around temple festivals, weddings and funerals, all of which require contributions of money and time Shobha can ill afford but cannot refuse. They visit the Maramma temple on the edge of town every month, and during Ugadi and Dasara they travel to her husband's ancestral village for puja and a family meal. Shobha's mother-in-law is devout and insists on Friday fasts and daily prayers; Shobha herself prays more out of habit than deep conviction, though she lights a lamp every evening and asks for her children's well-being. Her husband is part of a local savings group—a small chit fund—and Shobha joined a women's self-help group three years ago; it meets once a month and has lent her ₹10,000 at low interest, which helped pay for her son's school uniform and books. The SHG also organised a one-day visit to the Channapatna GI-tag office, where officials talked about protecting the craft's reputation, but Shobha is sceptical that a geographical-indication tag will bring her higher wages.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Shobha's family has ration cards and both children have Aadhaar cards; they collect rice and kerosene from the fair-price shop every month under Anna Bhagya. Her husband receives occasional MGNREGA work on road repair when the auto business is slow, though he complains the wage payment is delayed by months. Shobha has heard of the Gruha Jyoti and Gruha Lakshmi schemes but her household does not benefit much: their electricity use is minimal and the ₹2,000-per-month Gruha Lakshmi payment goes to her mother-in-law as the household head, not to Shobha herself. The Shakti free-bus scheme, though, has changed her life—she now travels to Ramanagara or Bengaluru occasionally for shopping or to visit relatives without worrying about the fare, and her daughter can reach tuition classes safely. Shobha has never met the local MLA, though his photo hangs in the taluk office and the workshop owner went to him once to complain about import duties. She voted in the 2023 Assembly election and the 2024 Lok Sabha poll but cannot recall the candidates' names; her husband tells her which party to support and she follows his advice, though she wishes the government would do more to protect Channapatna's toy industry from Chinese competition. Property tax and water bills are her husband's responsibility; she knows little about gram panchayat meetings or town politics.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Shobha is proud that Channapatna toys carry a GI tag and that the craft is known across India, but she worries the work will not last another generation—orders are falling, younger people are leaving for Bengaluru's factories and malls, and her own workshop may close if business does not improve. She blames cheap imports and government indifference in equal measure: why give us a GI tag, she asks, if you let foreign toys flood the market? She is determined that her children will study and find salaried jobs, not depend on craft work that pays so little and offers no security. She resents that Bengaluru, only an hour away on the new expressway, is booming while Channapatna's economy shrinks, and she wishes the government would bring a garment factory or some other industry to the town so women like her could earn more and work in better conditions. She worries about her daughter's marriage and the dowry she will need to arrange; she worries about her mother-in-law's health and the cost of medicines; she worries about the borewell loan and the auto loan and what will happen if her husband falls sick or the auto breaks down. Despite it all, she takes satisfaction in keeping her household running, in her children's school marks, and in the small savings she has managed to set aside in the SHG account, hidden from immediate need. She hopes her daughter will remember that her mother painted toys so she could study.
